analysis.one_liner: Bans raising oil and gas prices more than 15% during federally declared disasters.
analysis.headline: The bill was never voted on: introduced by one senator with no cosponsors in September 2005, after Hurricane Katrina, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita drove gasoline prices sharply higher, this bill would have made it a federal crime, during any presidentially declared major disaster or emergency, to raise the price of oil or gas products more than 15% above their pre-disaster level — unless the seller could show the increase came from higher costs or national and international market trends. Violating companies could face criminal fines up to $10 million and officers up to 3 years in prison; the Federal Trade Commission could also levy daily civil penalties, and state attorneys general could sue. Consumers could report suspected gouging through an FTC hotline and website.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, households, and businesses in disaster-declared areas, who would be protected from sudden fuel price spikes of more than 15% during and after emergencies like hurricanes, when many have no way to shop around or stock up.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and households hit by disasters

how_it_helps.text: During any federally declared natural disaster or emergency, sellers could not raise oil or gas prices more than 15% above the pre-disaster price, unless the increase was due to the seller's added costs or national and international market trends.

Violations would be a felony: corporations could be fined up to $10 million and individuals up to $350,000 or up to 3 years in prison, with the FTC able to add civil penalties of up to $5,000 per day of violation.
State attorneys general could sue violators on behalf of their states, and the FTC would set up a website link and toll-free number so consumers could report suspected gouging.

analysis.who_pays: Oil producers, refiners, wholesalers, and gas stations, which would face felony-level fines and prison exposure for raising prices more than 15% during declared disasters, even if the increase tracked genuine supply disruptions — though they could avoid penalties by showing added costs or market trends.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil producers, refiners, and fuel sellers

drawbacks.text: A hard price cap during a disaster could discourage suppliers from rushing extra fuel into a damaged region, since hauling gas into a hurricane zone costs more and the 15% ceiling may not cover it — the very shortages a cap tries to prevent could get worse if legitimate cost increases are hard to document.

The bill's civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation is small compared with what price-gouging can earn a large company, so without criminal prosecution the fines might function as a cost of doing business.

Determining whether a price increase reflects 'national or international market trends' versus local opportunism would be difficult to prove, and the federal cap could overlap or conflict with state anti-gouging laws.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in a disaster zone, the protection is real: fuel is an emergency necessity and a 15% cap, with serious criminal penalties behind it, targets the worst spikes. The strongest objection is that caps can worsen shortages if suppliers stop delivering into the disaster area, and that genuine cost increases are hard to separate from opportunism. On balance the bill addressed a narrow, recurring harm — post-disaster fuel spikes of the kind that followed Hurricane Katrina — with meaningful penalties, though a low daily civil fine would have left the criminal route as the main deterrent.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced by a single senator in September 2005 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it was never considered, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 19, 2005, in the weeks following Hurricane Katrina, when fuel price spikes in the affected region were a national controversy.
It had no cosponsors — Senator Dayton was its only supporter listed.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and the committee took no further action on it.
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, without the bill ever receiving a committee markup or a floor vote, so it died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers, refiners, wholesalers, and station owners are better off: no federal penalty or price ceiling applies to raising fuel prices during declared disasters, and companies keep the freedom to price however the market allows in an emergency.

for.name: Sen. Mark Dayton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in September 2005, in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina, and was its only sponsor; no senator cosponsored it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 19, 2005, and never scheduled a markup or reported it, leaving it to die at the end of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, and the bill had a single Democratic sponsor with no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers, refiners, and fuel wholesalers
industries.note: The bill would expose them to felony fines up to $10 million, prison terms for executives, and daily civil penalties for raising prices more than 15% during federally declared disasters. The exemption for added costs and market trends limits the hit, but the criminal exposure applies to a core pricing decision.

Small stations raising prices during a disaster could face the same felony penalties as large companies, though a $350,000 fine cap for non-corporate defendants and the cost-and-market-trends exemption give them room to justify genuine increases.
